text: — Dravichkata, gentlemen, tells stories so well that it will be hard to please you with a tale after him. And to tell you the truth, I also know a thing or two about Bai Ganyo — Vasil spoke up. — From Moscow, from Petersburg!
— Get on with it already, stop beating around the bush! — Dravichkata replied.
— The word "twisted" doesn't strike me as extraordinarily poetic — Mato joked.
— Quiet now, gentlemen. Vasil! Come on, my dear fellow, begin!

— On the way to Petersburg — Vasil began — we stopped at the station in Vilno. We were traveling together as a pair — Bay Ganyo and I. We went into the buffet. Bay Ganyo insisted that I treat him, since I had been smoking his tobacco along the way. I ordered beer and a snack. The buffet manager listened to our conversation, realized, it seemed, that I was Bulgarian, and asked us in Russian: — Excuse me, gentlemen, I believe you are Bulgarians?
We answered him affirmatively.
— Don't you know Mr. Dimitrov, the student?
— I don't know him, do you know him, Bay Ganyo!
— Dimitrova? Wait... aha! I remember. Dimitrov, I know, I know him. A sharp lad, I know him, of course!
— Can't you tell me where he is now? — asked the innkeeper.
— He is in Constantinople now — replied Bay Ganyo — he’ll be getting married there in a week. He’s hit the jackpot!
— Wh-at! — cried the innkeeper, as if thunderstruck. — He is to be mar-ried? Why, he was married here, gentlemen!...
— You bet. Look, ha, ha, ha! — Bay Ganyo cackled heartily. The innkeeper looked at him in wonder.
— You don't know him — continued Bay Ganyo, turning to me, — he's an awfully sharp kid, that Dimitrov...

I promised the innkeeper that as soon as I reached Petersburg, I would inform a gentleman who, I was certain, would immediately telegraph the Exarchate. I settled my bill. We boarded the train and set off for Petersburg.
— You just had to go and interfere — Bay Ganyo said to me reproachfully, — how do you know what sort of woman his wife here is.

We were traveling in third class. Bay Ganyo took up two seats and lay down to take a nap. At the next station, several more passengers entered our carriage and the extra seats had to be yielded to them, but Bay Ganyo is no fool — he pretends to be asleep and snores and snores. A giant of a German, a peasant, approached Bay Ganyo with a bag in hand and began to wake him, nudging him lightly on his boots. Bay Ganyo keeps quiet and just lets out a *hrrr... puff... hrrr... puff...* and, having covered his face from the German, winks at me, as if to say, "look how clever I am." "Nu, get up!" the German shouted and began to poke my companion quite palpably. *Hrrr... puff!...* "Nu, don't pretend, you devil!" the German growled and with one sweep brushed aside Bay Ganyo's legs, sent him tumbling over his saddlebags, and sat down with us. Bay Ganyo pretended to be startled, rubbed his eyes, and immediately, as if nothing had happened, took out his cigarette case and offered it open to the German: "Bulgarian tobacco!"
— Ah, so you're Bulgarians! Very pleased to meet you — the German said good-naturedly and began to roll himself a cigarette. — You're going to Piter. Me too. Together, then.

As soon as we arrived in St. Petersburg, I hastened to fulfill the promise I had made to the innkeeper in Vilno. I met with an acquaintance of mine and told him about Dimitrov’s escapade. He immediately telegraphed Constantinople and managed to stop the impending wedding. He, in turn, told me the rest of the story about the deaf-mute boy. It is not known when or how he had been coached to run away from Vilno, but one day he arrived in St. Petersburg, where for a long time he was the victim of the basest exploitation by Dimitrov, who not only pocketed the sums sent by the unfortunate boy’s brother but also forced the poor child to go from door to door, visiting all the more influential figures and well-known philanthropists in St. Petersburg to beg for money. And not only in St. Petersburg, but he often sent him as far as Kronstadt, to the famous saint of the common folk, John of Kronstadt...
Having almost no means of subsistence, I was forced to live in the Deshovka, a refuge for the poorest of students. Bay Ganyo most energetically insisted on coming to the Deshovka as well.
— Look, you can’t, Bai Ganyo, this place is only for students.
— So what if it’s for students — Bay Ganyo was trying to convince me, — aren’t students people like me? Is it such a big deal if they take in a Bulgarian for once?
— But you are a rich man, Bay Ganyo, you can afford to pay for a hotel.

— What a simpleton you are — Bay Ganyo reproached me, — I thought you were shrewder. Hey there, fellow Bulgarian, why should we give our money to the Muscovites? If you stumble upon a windfall, grab it with both hands! How are they to know what my situation is?
— It’s not possible, Bay Ganyo; the poor students will protest, they’ll be angry with me, and they might even kick me out of the dormitory.

— Stubborn Bulgarian head! — Bay Ganyo continued. — Don't you have a tongue in your head? Aren't you sharp enough to tell them that I'm your brother, that I'm a man in distress; why, it's enough just to say I'm Bulgarian—you know what simpletons those Russians are!...
— No, no, I can't! — I cried out resolutely and started toward Deshovka.

— Oho! You think you’ll shake me off that easily! Just you wait! You haven't seen anything yet! — Bay Ganyo grumbles, following behind me. — A Bulgarian! And he calls himself a Bulgarian! Not a penny's worth of patriotism!... Wait up, man, don't rush so much, I can't catch up with you, my saddlebags are heavy! Wait up, fellow Bulgarian!...

At that moment, we must have presented quite a curious sight, for the people passing by on the sidewalks turned and looked at us intently. Bay Ganyo was ten paces behind me, his saddlebags slung over his shoulder on his cane, his rug draped over his other arm, which he raised every now and then to wipe his sweaty brow. His fur cap was barely clinging to the crown of his head. Bay Ganyo strode after me, grumbling: "Wait, for God's sake, man, at least take the rug, it's breaking my arm... You think you can shake me off! You don't know what a piece of work your Bay Ganyo is!..." I was treading carefully, calculating in my mind how I would show up with Bay Ganyo at Deshovka’s and how I would justify this impulsive move. I’ll have to lie! And yet I saw that shaking him off was unthinkable! Finally, since it was only a matter of a few days, I reluctantly resigned myself to the situation. And Bay Ganyo kept walking and walking behind me, still grumbling, but he dropped his tough-guy talk and began in a minor key: "Listen here, Bay Vasil, wait a moment, please, Bay Vasil, we're Bulgarians after all..."

And imagine, gentlemen, at that moment I felt sorry for Bay Ganyo! Believe me! I was aware that his conduct was outrageous, that he was a disgusting miser, an egoist, a cunning trickster, a hypocritical exploiter, a brute and a vulgarian to the marrow of his bones... but I felt sorry for him: in the subtle vibrations of the tone with which he uttered those last words, my ear caught a tender note that had been hidden and remains hidden in Bay Ganyo’s heart, but rarely — God, how rarely! — does it appear... I do not know, it may seem ridiculous to you, unnatural, but I will tell you, gentlemen, that at that moment I looked upon Bay Ganyo differently; as if someone whispered to me: “Do not despise this simple, cunning, poor wretch; he is a child of a crude environment, he is a victim of crude educators; the evil does not reside in him himself, but in the influence of the surrounding environment. Bay Ganyo is active, sensible, receptive — above all, receptive! Place him under the influence of a good guide, and you will see what feats he is capable of performing. Bay Ganyo has so far manifested only his animal energy, but within him lies a great store of potential spiritual power, which awaits only a moral impulse to be transformed into a living force...”

We arrived at the Deshovka. Most of the students had not yet returned from vacation, so there were plenty of vacant spots. My bed had been saved by my faithful comrade Kocho, an Albanian, a pauper in the highest degree, who received three rubles a month from the Slavic Society for tea and sugar; he had entered the university, studied there for two years, but having convinced himself that it was not for him, he left and entered the seminary. This Kocho was a good man, he would give his life for a friend, but God forbid you should provoke him—in an instant all his Arnaut passions would boil over, he would turn pale, then green, his eyes would fill with blood, a total beast!... When Bay Ganyo and I entered the room, we found Kocho in a horizontal position on the bed: on that bed, it was difficult to tell at a glance which was the pillow, which the bedding, and which the blanket... Kocho leapt from his bed with the agility of a panther, embraced me, kissed me, met Bay Ganyo, and cheerful, grinning from ear to ear with joy, arranged for us to sit, one on the bed, another on a trunk, while apologizing for the slight disorder in the room. Then he opened the door and let out an Arnaut cry: "Vanka, put on the samovar, my dear fellow!"—"What do you need a samovar for when there's no tea or sugar!" the "dear fellow" called back from the end of the corridor. Kocho grabbed his head with both hands, paced across the room, snatched his hat, and without listening to our pleas to stay, saying that we would buy tea and sugar, he tore himself away, shouted "right away," and vanished... Bay Ganyo and I waited for half an hour, we waited for a whole hour—Kocho did not return. Something must have happened to him.

So as not to waste the fine day, I suggested to Bay Ganyo that we go out for a walk. "Hey, wait, let’s wait a bit, the man will treat us to tea," Bay Ganyo objected; he couldn’t let a freebie pass him by, no matter where it came from. But I insisted nonetheless. Bay Ganyo stuffed the vials into his sash, and we went out. As we approached the Anichkov Bridge, we heard from afar a beastly shout, mixed with the most desperate curses and insults; we reached the bridge, and what did we see!... Kocho, enraged like a tiger, had sunk his iron fingers into the neck of an unknown gentleman whose hat was rolling on the stones; he had bent the man’s head down and was struggling to throw him off the bridge. The victim was making every effort to escape, but it was not so easy to tear oneself away from the hands of the maddened Arnaut. "Charlatan!" Kocho roared. "Scoundrel! Villain! You’re the spy, not me, you’re the spy, you son of a bitch! I’ll kill you, you vile creature!" I rushed to break them up. Bay Ganyo shouted after me: "Leave them alone, man, why do you need trouble on your head, let them smash each other’s heads; leave them, they’ll drag you as a witness to the police stations." I did not heed Bay Ganyo’s advice and headed toward the Arnaut, who did not stop tearing his throat and spewing the most shameful epithets at his victim, whom he had already dragged to the edge of the bridge, and it seemed to me, one more moment—and the stranger would fly headfirst into the clear waters of the Fontanka. "Charlatan! Scoundrel!" Kocho roared, sinking his bony fingers even deeper into his opponent’s thick neck.

When I was just a few steps away from them, the victim, terrified by his impending doom, made a desperate move, wrenched himself from the Albanian's grasp, instantly snatched up his soiled hat, and bolted. "Stop, you charlatan! You filthy coward, you scoundrel!" Kocho grabbed a stone and hurled it after him. The stranger ran to a tram, hopped inside, and vanished... But the Albanian would not be pacified. "I’ll kill you, you vile charlatan!" he continued to growl, shaking his fist at the empty space where his enemy had disappeared. I called Kocho by name; he turned, but did not recognize me!... There was something beastly in his gaze; his eyes gleamed, his face had turned a sallow, dark hue, his teeth chattered as if in a violent fever, and his lips quivered convulsively, letting out a low growl. "V... v... b... r... r... Char-r-rl... S-s-son of a... b... scoundrel... m... m... m... Charlatan!" he cried out once more, turning threateningly toward his invisible foe. "Kocho, my dear fellow, what happened to you? Who was that gentleman?" I asked with friendly sympathy. He fixed his eyes on me, staring blankly and maliciously, and still he did not recognize me!... "I’ll kill you, you vile creature! I’ll show you who’s a spy!" Kocho growled, shaking his fist at a passing tram, as if his enemy were sitting in every single one of them.

"Kocho, please, tell me what happened to you," I pleaded with my friend, who was driven to a frenzy of rage. "Who was that gentleman?" Kocho looked at me once more and cried out: "That man is the greatest scoundrel! Do you understand? The grea-test scoun-drel!" — and he turned his eyes away again, returning to his outburst of curses. I began to suspect that my friend was the victim of some treachery devised by his enemy, but exactly what it was, I did not and could not fathom. What Kocho told me was so utterly vile that it defied all conjecture.

We managed to calm Kocho down after a fashion and went with him into a tavern to drink tea. We lingered there for quite a long time, engrossed in the Albanian's stories about Aslanov's humiliating escapades. Even Bay Ganyo did not venture to shout his "bravo!" or "ashkolsun!"; on the contrary, from time to time he clicked his tongue, shook his head in wonder, and said: "My, what a total ass this man was!" We left the tavern and set off along Nevsky Prospekt. A mixed crowd from all parts of the world filled the sidewalks of the brilliant street; we could barely weave our way through the passers-by. All sorts of carriages moved along the street in two rows. Shops, each more luxurious than the last, enticed the eyes of the public. Bay Ganyo deigned to express the opinion that "after all, even Petersburg isn't such a bad place"... For a whole hour, we pushed through the crowd until we reached the Neva. As soon as we came out onto the quieter English Embankment, before we had even taken ten steps, Kocho gave my sleeve a startled tug and cried out in a choked voice: "There he is!"
— Who?
— The charlatan!
— Which charlatan?

— The Most High! Stop! Let’s hide so he doesn’t notice us! — he muttered and pulled us by the sleeves behind the columns of a gateway. Bay Ganyo poked his nose out from behind the column and looked in the direction indicated by Kocho.
— Who do you see? — asks Kocho.
— I see a man — Bay Ganyo whispers mysteriously. — Hey, Vasil, take a look, this man looks a lot like our Dondukov-Korsakov.
— He is the same — Kocho replies — who else do you see?

— I see two more people, kneeling before Dondukov, look! Tsk... tsk... tsk... they are kissing his boots, weeping, begging him for something, beating their chests, look! Tsk... tsk... tsk... he wants to shake them off, but they won't let him go — one on this side, the other on that, clutching his legs...
— Look closely, can't you recognize any of them? — the Albanian dictated.

— I can't, how am I to recognize them, they keep knocking their heads against his boots... Ha, wait — said Bai Ganyo, — wait!... I've recognized him! Why, it's him... for real! Why, it's that fellow, the one you were going to throw off the bridge... it's him!
— He is the same... the scoundrel! You are now witnesses to one of his wretched comedies! — the Arnaut growled through clenched teeth. — Now, let’s slip back onto Nevsky Prospect.
— Wait, let's see the end of the scene — I stated.

— There is no need — Kocho said decisively, — the outcome is certain: they will cling to his legs and weep until he gives them a few rubles, or a recommendation to another victim, or some intercession... These scoundrels are capable of disgracing the name of an entire nation...
— Goodness! This fellow is a total ass — cried Bay Ganyo, clicking his tongue.
— Well, why did you stop, Vasil? Keep going! — one of the group called out.
— Tell me about the story with Ermolova...
— Forget it, I'm disgusted — Vasil stated.
— Or about Princess Belozerskaya...
— Forget it, I can't take it anymore!
— Well, do you know the story of Bay Ganyo and the tripe soup? — another one chimed in.
— Well, do you know anything about the shaved mustaches...

— Enough, gentlemen! There is no end to these Bay Ganyo stories. Let’s start the second part of the gathering already. Marcus Aurelius, sing something, my little dove! Or you, Kalina-Malina, sing a little something!... Come on: “Roll u-u-up, Velo girl, your white slee-ee-ves...”
The second part of the party began... After midnight we dispersed.

Goodbye, Bay Ganyo! Travel across Europe, carry to every corner the product of our beautiful Rose Valley and... I beg of you, Bay Ganyo, look a little deeper into European life, may you see its true face; enough of that cursed reverse side has been thrust upon you!...
